'''Robert Anderson Ellis Jr.''' (1927 – 15 December 1989) was an American physicist and head of experimental projects at the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Bol |first1=Kees |last2=Furth |first2=Harold P. |last3=Gottlieb |first3=Melvin B. |last4=Spitzer |first4=Lyman |last5=Stix |first5=Thomas H. |last6=Yamada |first6=Masaaki |last7=Van Allen |first7=James A. |title=Robert A. Ellis Jr |journal=Physics Today |date=March 1991 |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=86–88 |doi=10.1063/1.2810048 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Robert Ellis was born in [[Kansas City, Missouri]].<ref name=":1">{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|531861159}} |title=AMONG TOP 73 PHYSICISTS:: Robert A. Ellis attends national science meeting |newspaper=Afro-American |date=2 January 1954 |page=5 }}</ref>

Ellis received a bachelor's degree from [[Fisk University]] in 1948, and a master's degree from [[Yale University]] in 1949. After completing his master's education, Ellis began work as an instructor at the [[Tennessee State University|Tennessee Agricultural & Industrial State College]], in [[Nashville, Tennessee]] (now [[Tennessee State University]]).<ref name=":0" />

While on leave from his instructor position, Ellis began doctoral studies at the [[University of Iowa]]. [[James Van Allen]] was Ellis' advisor, and Ellis was Van Allen's first doctoral student. At Iowa, Ellis also worked as a research assistant.<ref name=":1" />

Ellis' thesis was titled "Low momentum end of the spectrum of heavy primary cosmic rays," and was published in February 1954.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ellis |first1=Robert Anderson |title=Low Momentum End of the Spectrum of Heavy Primary Cosmic Rays |date=1954 |oclc=48446584 }}{{page needed|date=April 2023}}</ref>

== Career ==
[[File:US-Iowa-Deacon-rocket-1952.jpg|thumb|A model Deacon rocket with payload, representative of those used to test the ionosphere. Ellis is second from the right.]]
After completing his PhD, Ellis returned to his instructor position at Tennessee Agricultural & Industrial State College, where he was later promoted to full professor.<ref name=":0" /> In 1954, he was invited as one of 73 "outstanding physicists" to take part in the Cosmic Ray Conference, sponsored by [[Duke University]] and the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name=":1" /> The same year, he joined a research team with [[James Van Allen]] and [[Melvin B. Gottlieb]] that traveled to the Arctic to investigate cosmic ray activity in the polar region. In a report on this trip, Ellis was credited with the development of balloon launched rocket techniques.<ref>{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|531866973}} |title=Prepares for Arctic trip: Dr. R. A. Ellis to probe cosmic ray |newspaper=Afro-American |date=19 June 1954 |page=5 }}</ref>

In 1956, Ellis joined [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory|Project Matterhorn]], a Princeton-based working group focused on controlled fusion studies.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Robert A. Ellis - Physicist of the African Diaspora |url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/physics/ellis-roberta.html |access-date=2023-03-09 |website=www.math.buffalo.edu}}</ref> In his work within Project Matterhorn, Ellis focused on magnetic confinement and heating of plasmas in [[stellarator]]s. The group's studies on B-1 and B-3 devices were the first to document ohmic heating; anomalous transport across the magnetic field; radio frequency plasma heating at the lower-hybrid frequency; and nonlinear cyclotron harmonic interactions.<ref name=":0" />
[[File:HD.6D.745 (13471450163).jpg|alt=Schematic of the Adiabatic Toroidal Compressor (ATC)|thumb|Schematic of the Adiabatic Toroidal Compressor (ATC)]]
Project Matterhorn was led by [[Lyman Spitzer|Lyman Spitzer, Jr.]], and after the termination of nuclear weapons research in 1958, in 1961 the project was declassified and renamed the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]] (PPPL).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Timeline |url=https://www.pppl.gov/timeline |access-date=2023-03-09 |website=Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Project Matterhorn |url=https://nuclearprinceton.princeton.edu/project-matterhorn |access-date=2023-03-09 |website=Nuclear Princeton |language=en}}</ref>

In 1969, Ellis spent six months at the Institute of Nuclear Physics in [[Novosibirsk|Novosibirsk, USSR]], with a focus on fostering international collaboration in the sciences. Ellis also served as foreign secretary of the Advisory Committee on the USSR and Eastern Europe for the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=":0" />

From 1972 to 1976, Ellis was the group leader for the Adiabatic Toroidal Compressor [[tokamak]] at [[Princeton University]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Administration |date=7 February 2020 |title=The National Society of Black Physicists honors Dr. Robert A. Ellis Jr. |url=https://nsbp.org/blogpost/1904681/362806/February-7-2020 |access-date=9 March 2023}}</ref> This device was used in fusion experiments for the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|U.S. Atomic Energy Commission]] at PPPL from 1972 to 1977. It was the first tokamak without a copper liner.

During his career, Ellis was a member of the Department of Energy's Compact Toroid Coordination Committee, in which he and Japanese [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] physicist [[Masaaki Yamada]] led the [[Spheromak]] project.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> Other professional appointments included:

* Member, the Science Advisory Committee for [[NASA]] Research Laboratories (1976-1978)
* Head of the physics section of the International Atomic Energy Agency in [[Vienna|Vienna, Austria]] (two years)
* U.S. representative to the Commission on Plasma Physics of the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Physics]] (1984)<ref name=":0" />

In 1988, Ellis began as head of experimental projects at PPPL, where he would work until his death in 1989. In this role, he was responsible for all non-TFTR experimental work.<ref name=":3" />

== Personal life ==
Robert Ellis married fellow Tennessee State University professor Victoria Toms while they were both teaching there. Together they moved to New Jersey for his research job.<ref>"[https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2024/06/lynching-great-migration-mississippi-south/678212/ The Lynching That Sent My Family North]" by Ko Bragg, ''The Atlantic'', June 2024. Accessed June 8, 2024.</ref>

Robert Ellis's son, Bob Ellis, is also a physicist. Bob Ellis studied at [[Princeton University]] and the [[New Jersey Institute of Technology]], and is currently chief engineer at the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]].<ref name=":3" /> The father and son duo briefly worked together in the PPPL in 1981, when Robert Ellis, Jr., headed the S-1 [[Spheromak]] and Bob Ellis worked on S-1 before moving to TFTR to work on diagnostics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bob Ellis: New chief engineer at PPPL has designed components for fusion experiments around the world |url=https://www.newswise.com/articles/bob-ellis-new-chief-engineer-at-pppl-has-designed-components-for-fusion-experiments-around-the-world |access-date=2023-03-09 |website=www.newswise.com |language=en}}</ref>

Ellis died December 15, 1989, in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], from [[kidney failure]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=1989-12-23 |title=Robert A. Ellis Jr., former TSU physics professor, dies in N.J. |pages=15 |work=[[The Tennessean]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-tennessean-obituary-for-robert-a-el/77768283/}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
[[Princeton University]] sponsors a fellowship honoring Robert A. Ellis that is awarded at the [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=jfasano |date=2020-07-31 |title=Accomplished early career physicist is first recipient of fellowship that honors pioneering PPPL physicist Robert Ellis Jr. |url=https://pwb.princeton.edu/2020/07/31/accomplished-early-career-physicist-is-first-recipient-of-fellowship-that-honors-pioneering-pppl-physicist-robert-ellis-jr/ |access-date=2023-03-09 |website=Princeton Weekly Bulletin |language=en-US}}</ref>
